claudo (* clōdo:
clodunt ita (oculos),; but some refer clodo to claudeo; and more freq., although not in Cic., clūdo, as always in the compounds; v.infra), si, sum, 3, v. a.
root sklu-, klu-, to shut; cf. κλείω, κλείς, clavis; O. H. Germ. scliuzu; M. H. Germ. schliessen; also claudus, clavus
, to shut.
To shut something that is open, to close, shut up (opp. aperire; freq. in prose and poetry).
Claudo: forem cubiculi,; cf. ; and, clausae fores,; : conventus portus Varroni clausit,: januam serā,: domum,: ostia,: portas,; ; cf. : omnes aditus,; ; : rivos,to dam up,: ad claudendas pupulas, ne quid incideret, et ad aperiendas, etc.,: ocellos (in dying), so, oculos,: lumina,; : clausis foribus,.—
Cludo: domum,: Janum Quirinum ter clusit,; : animam clusit dolor,.—
Trop.: nec ita claudenda est res familiaris, ut eam benignitas aperire non possit,: domus clausa contra cupiditatem,: habere domum clausam pudori et sanctimoniae, patentem cupiditati et voluptatibus,; cf. : aures ad doctissimas voces,; cf. : cludendae sunt aures malis vocibus,: horum ferocia vocem Euandri clausit,: fugam hostibus, q. s. to block up, to cut off, prevent, ; so : alicui iter,; : alios incessus,: sideritis sanguinem claudit,i. e. stops, stanches,: cluso corpore adversum vim veneni,: clausa consilia habere,i. e. to conceal,; cf. ; ; ; .— Poet.: animam laqueo, i. e. to end one's life, (cf.: vitalesque vias et respiramina clausit,).—
To close, end, conclude (so, except the milit. expression, agmen, only poet. or in post-Aug. prose; most freq. in Quint.).
Claudo: cujus octavum trepidavit aetas Claudere lustrum,: opus,: jus,: labores ingentis belli,: epistulam,; , 242: cenas lactucā,; : cum ventum est ad ipsum illud, quo veteres tragoediae comoediaeque clauduntur, Plaudite,; cf. ; .—
Cludo: cludere bella,: cludendi incohandique sententias ratio,; cf. opp. incipere, (as claudere, opp. incipere, ): cum versus cluditur,; cf. ; ; ; 9, 4, 93; 9, 4, 102; 9, 4, 104; 9, 4, 105; 12, 10, 31.—
Agmen, in milit. lang., to close the procession or train, to bring up the rear, ; ; ; so, aciem,; cf. cogo, I. B. 3.—
(For the compounds includo, concludo.) Claudere aliquid aliquā re, to shut up or in something by something, to enclose, encompass, surround, imprison, hide, confine (class., esp. freq. in poetry and in the historians).
Claudo, with abl.: locum aquā,: quae (Syracusarum urbs) loci naturā terrā marique clauderetur,: (animae) clausae tenebris et carcere caeco,: stabulis armenta,: claudens textis cratibus pecus,; cf. ; : ensem vaginā,: aliquem Gyaro,; : clausus domo,; cf.: intra domum,: rivus praealtis utrimque clausus ripis,; cf. ; ; : clauditur cubiculo aliquis,; cf.: in atras et profundas tenebras eum claudebant, Tubero ap. : in arcā,: claudam in curiā vos,: in tectis,: (apes) in arbore inani,: aquilonem in antris,.—Without abl.: nihil se tam clausum posse habere, quod non istius cupiditati apertissimum esset,: insula ea sinum ab alto claudit,; cf. ; ; —In milit. lang., of a hostile encompassing, to encompass, invest, besiege, blockade, etc.: praestare arbitrabatur, unum locum... quam omnia litora ac portus custodiā clausos teneri,: urbem operibus,; ; cf.: urbem obsidione,: adversarios locorum angustiis,; cf. ; : multitudine,: hinc Tusco claudimur amni,are hemmed in,.—So of hunting: nemorum saltus,: indagine collis,: silvas vastasque feras indagine,; : insidiis altas valles,: cur tibi clauduntur rete Imbelles capr eae,.—
Cludo, : venti clusi Nubibus,; .—
Trop.: numcubi meam Benignitatem sensisti in te claudier?: nolo tibi ullum commodum in me claudier,; cf. I. A. 2. supra.—Esp. of speech and rhythm: qui non claudunt numeris sententias,; : pedibus verba,i. e. to compose verses,; cf. : quod clausae hieme Alpes essent,; cf. : rura gelu tum claudit hiems (and : illos aspera ponti interclusit hiems).—Hence, P.a. as subst.: clausum (clūsum), i, n., an enclosed place (for confining or keeping any thing): clausa effringere,: in clauso linquere,in confinement,: fructus clauso custodire,, praef. § 3: sub uno clauso,: clausa domorum,: clausa viarum,.

,

Prop.: sutor,: deus,: claudus altero pede,; : pes,: pars serpentis,. 278 al.—
Prov.: iste claudus, quemadmodum aiunt, pilam,said of one who cannot make a right use of a thing,.—

la:verb:clamo.gloss: to cry out, clamor, shout, yell, exclaim
senses: to cry out, clamor, shout, yell, exclaim
to address as, call by name
la:verb:clamo.html:
clāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
[Sanscr. kar-, to celebrate; Gr. καλέω, κλητός; cf.: clarus, classis, nomenclator, concilium].
Neutr., to call, cry out, shout aloud, to complain with a loud voice, vociferari (class. and very freq.; mostly of human beings): populus convolat; Tumultuantur, clamant, pugnant de loco, prol. alt. 33: dic mihi, Non clamas? non insanis?; cf. ; : clamare de pecuniā,—Of a vehement bawling before a tribunal: qui quid in dicendo posset, numquam satis attendi: in clamando quidem video eum esse bene robustum atque exercitatum,.—In comedy, of snoring: dormit Sceledrus intus? Lu. Non naso quidem: Nam eo magnum clamat,—
Transf., of animals and things; of geese: anseres, qui tantummodo clamant, nocere non possunt,.—Of the chirping of a cricket: (cicada) multo validius clamare occoepit,.—Of the roaring of waters, the rustling of trees, etc., ; ; : clamant amnes, freta, nubila silvae,.— Also of abstract things (cf. under II. B.): et non ulla meo clamat in ore fides?i. e. does my sincerity never plainly proclaim itself in my voice?.—But esp. freq.,
Act., to call or cry aloud to something or some one, to proclaim, declare, to invoke, call upon, etc., = exclamare; constr. with acc. of the person or thing, or a clause as object, in direct and (more freq.) in indirect discourse.
With acc.: e somno pueros clamo, Lucil. ap. P.; so, janitorem,: comites,: matrem ore,; cf.: ora clamantia nomen,; 11, 665: morientem nomine,.—With two accs.: se causam crimenque,: me deum,te insanum,: aliquem furem,; .—With acc. rei: divūm atque hominum fidem,: aquas,triumphum,: Saturnalia,: pulchre! bene! recte!.—
With a clause as object, in direct discourse (mostly poet.): ad me omnes clamant: Janua culpa tua est,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; —
With a clause as object, in indirect discourse: clamant omnes indignissime Factum esse,: quid facto esset opus puerperae... illis clamat de viā,; : solos felices viventes clamat in urbe,.—
With final clause: clamare coeperunt, sibi ut haberet hereditatem,; : clamans in hostem, ne rex Croesus occideretur,.—
Trop., of abstract things, to proclaim, declare: quom mi ipsum nomen ejus Archidemides Clamaret dempturum esse, si quid crederem,; cf.: eum ipsum (sc. Regulum) clamat virtus beatiorem fuisse quam potantem in rosā Thorium,; : quae (tabulae) se corruptas atque interlitas esse clamant,; : quid enim restipulatio clamat?; ; cf. clamito, Il.
la:verb:clamo.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

la:noun:clientela.html:
clĭentēla, ae, f.
id.
,
the relation of patron and client, clientship; patronage, protection; the intimate and reciprocal duties of attachment and interest, based on the private relations in Rome between a Roman of a lower grade (plebeian or freedman) or a foreigner, and the patron chosen by him (cf. Dion. Halic. 2, 9 and 10, pp. 83- 85; ; ): Thais patri se commendavit in clientelam et fidem, * ; cf.: esse in fide et clientelā. to be the client of, : conferre se in fidem et clientelam alicujus,: scis quam diligam Siculos et quam illam clientelam honestam judicem,

: per nomen et clientelas inlustrior haberi,.—

Very freq., mostly in plur., concrete, clients, dependents: amplissimas clientelas acceptas a majoribus confirmare poterit,; so : magna esse Pompei beneficia et magnas clientelas in provinciā sciebat,bodies of clients,; ; ; : incedentibus regiis clientelis,; 13, 37; 14, 61; ; .—In sing., . —
In gen., clientship, alliance (cf. cliens, B.), .—
Trop. (cf. cliens, II.), patronage, protection: poëtae sub clientelā musarum esse,.

senses: renowned, famous, famed, distinguished, illustrious, celebrated, glorious
la:adj:clarus.html:
clārus, a, um, adj.
kindr. with Germ. klar; Engl. clear; cf. clamo
,
clear, bright (opp. obscurus, caecus; very freq. in all periods, and in all kinds of composition).
Lit.
Relating to the sight, clear, bright, shining, brilliant, etc.
Absol.: luce clarā et candidā,: ut mulierum famam multorum oculis lux clara custodiat,open day,; cf.: frequentissimā celebritate et clarissimā luce laetari,: lumen,: oculorum lumina,; cf.: mundi lumina (i.e. sol et luna),: oculi,: incendia,: lucerna,: scintillae ignis,: fulmina,: vestis splendor,: color,; cf.: color clarissimus,: candor,: loca,: caelum,: nox,: pater omnipotens clarus intonat,in the clear sky, Serv.; cf. : sidus,: clarissimae gemmae,; cf. lapides,: vitrum,: purpurarum sidere clarior usus,.—
With abl.: speculo, dub.: argento clari delphines,: rutilis squamis,: ferrugine,; cf. Wagn.: auro gemmisque corona,; ; : albo Lucifer exit Clarus equo,: claraeque coruscis Fulguribus taedae, —*
Poet., of the wind (cf.: albus, candidus, and in Gr. λαμπρὸς ἄνεμος; v. Lidd. and Scott under λαμπρός), making clear, i. e. bringing fair weather: aquilo, Forbig. ad loc.—
Relating to the hearing, clear, loud, distinct: clarā voce vocare,; ; ; ; ; : lectio,: clariore voce,; cf. : sonor,: clamor,: plausus,: plangor,: latratus,: ictus,: strepitus, Luc.: vox (opp. obtusa),; Spald.: spiritus,; cf. and 82: syllabae clariores,.—
Trop.
Clear, manifest, plain, evident, intelligible (syn.: planus, apertus, perspicuus, dilucidus, etc.): vide ut mi haec certa et clara attuleris, Ruhnk.; cf.: omnia non properanti clara certaque erunt,: clara res est, quam dicturus sum, totā Siciliā celeberrima atque notissima,; ; : luce sunt clariora nobis tua consilia,: id quod est luce clarius,: si ea, quae dixi, sole ipso inlustriora et clariora sunt,; : caecis hoc satis clarum est,: lumen eloquentiae,; cf. ; : in narrando (T. Livius) clarissimi candoris, Spald. and Frotsch.: Massinissam regem post LXXXVI. annum generasse filium clarum est,: somno clarius,: exempla,; : documenta,.—
Brilliant, celebrated, renowned, illustrious, honorable, famous, glorious, etc. (cf.: illustris, insignis, eximius, egregius, praestans, nobilis; a favorite epithet, esp. in the sup., like fortissimus, designating the highest praise of the honor-loving Roman; hence, a standing title, at all times, of distinguished public characters, as consuls, proconsuls, pontifices, senators, etc.): nobilitas,; opp. to obscurus,; so : clari viri atque magni, Cato ap. ; : certe non tulit ullos haec civitas aut gloriā clariores, aut auctoritate graviores,: vir fortissimus et clarissimus,; cf. , § 153; ; : exempla clara et inlustria,: pugna clara et commemorabilis,: pax clarior majorque quam bellum fuerat,: animus abunde pollens potensque et clarus,; so, facundia clara pollensque,: clara et magnifica,: clari potentesque fieri,: familia,; : majores,: pater si in Equestri gradu clarus, clarior vitricus, Plin.

Ep. 2, 13, 4: clarissimi consules,: generis clarissimus auctor,: clarissima civitas,: apud Germanicos quoque (Titus),: scriptores,.—

With abl.: clariores gloriā,; v.supra: arte medicinae,: eloquendi suavitate,: sententiis,: Juppiter giganteo triumpho,: agendis causis,: Ajax toties servatis Achivis,: bello,; : gens memoriā nominis,: Cluvius Rufus eloquentiā,.—
With in: in arte tibiarum,; cf.: clarissimi in eā scientiā,: in litteris,: in agendo,: in foro,: in contionibus,; .—*
With ex: ex doctrinā nobilis et clarus,.—(ε) With ob: ob obscuram linguam,: ob id factum,; cf.: urbs clara ob insignem munimento naturali locum,.—(ζ) With ab: Trojanoque a sanguine clarus Acestes,.—(η) With gen.: artis ejus,.—
As a title: clarissimus vir,; cf. : clarissimi consules,; cf. ; ; Alex. Sev. 21 al.: permitto tibi vir clarissime Veiento (a senator), dicere,; so, ordo = senatorius,; cf. also .—
Meton., of the wives of such distinguished public characters: clarissimae feminae,.—
In a bad sense, notorious: minus clarum putavit fore quod de armario quam quod de sacrario esset ablatum,; ; : ecquid hoc totā Siciliā clarius, ecquid indignius? etc.,, § 16: populus (sc. Campanus), luxuriā superbiāque clarus,.—Hence, adv.: clārē (freq. and class.).
Lit.
Of sight (acc. to I. A.), brightly, clearly: clare oculis video,: clare fulgens caesaries,: occidere,of a star,.—Comp.: clarius micare,: nitere,. —Sup.: clarissime lucere,.—
Of hearing (acc. to I. B.), clearly, distinctly, plainly, aloud: clare recitare,: plaudite, id. Am. fin.; cf. id. Bacch. fin.: dic, Ruhnk.: gemere,: res clare enuntiare,: sonare,: exscreare,: maledicere, et saep.: palam et clare,; cf. .—Comp.: clarius fabulari,.—Sup.: pisces clarissime audiunt,; .—
Trop.
Mentally (acc. to II. A.), distinctly, intelligibly, clearly: clare atque evidenter ostendere,; cf. : aliquid intellegere,. —Comp.: eo clarius id periculum apparet, Cael. ap. ; so, clarius intellegi,: clarius elucebit,: clarius ostendemus,— Sup., .—
Morally (acc. to II. B.), illustriously, honorably (very rare): clarius exsplendescebat,.

senses: clemency, mildness (of climate or the weather)
Grace (capitalized for royal/imperial titles and addresses)
la:noun:clementia.html:
clēmentĭa, ae, f.
1. clemens
.
A calm, tranquil state of the elements, calmness, mildness, tranquillity (like clemens in this signif. mostly post-Aug.): clementia ventorum, tranquillitas maris,: soli caelique,; cf.: emollit gentes clementia caeli,: aestatis,: hiemis,: nascentis anni,: diei,: Nili,.—
(Acc. to clemens, II. B.) Indulgent, forbearing conduct towards the errors and faults of others, moderation, mildness, humanity, forbearance, benignity, clemency, mercy (the class. signif.; very freq., esp. in prose; syn.: benignitas, comitas, lenitas, mansuetudo, etc.): clementia (est), per quam animi temere in odium alicujus concitati invectio comitate retinetur,: clementia est temperantia animi in potestate ulciscendi, vel lenitas... in constituendis poenis,: facilitas et clementia, * ; cf. : illam clementiam mansuetudinemque nostri imperii tantam in crudelitatem inhumanitatemque esse conversam,; ; : lenitas et clementia,: clementia et probitas vestra, Dietsch; ; ; ; : juris, Spald., and antith. to jus asperius, ; opp. severitatem,: elephanti contra minus validos,: leonis in supplices,; and as an attribute of princes,; ; whence a title ofthe emperors, v. IV.—Less freq.,
Kindness, sympathy: satrapes violare clementiam quam regis opes minui maluit,.—
Clementia, personified as a deity, the goddess of grace, ; ; —
A title of the emperor: Clementia tua,Your Grace,; Spart. ap. Geta, I. init.

la:adv:clam.html:
clam (old access. form callim, or, acc. to Cod. Gu. 1, calam, Paul. ex Müll.) [root cal-; cf.: calix, celo, cella, occulo, caligo], adv. and prep.,
secretly, privately; and in the predicate after sum and fore, hidden, secret, unknown (opp. palam; except once in Caes., v. II. infra; in class. prose only used as adv.).
Adv.
In gen.: clamque palamque, Enn. ap. (247 Vahl.): ignis mortalibus clam Divisus, Att. ap. : mea nunc facinora aperiuntur, clam quae speravi fore,; cf. ; : nec id clam esse potuit,: clam mordax canis (Gr. λαθροδήκτης κύων), ; cf. ; ; ; cf. : clam peperit uxor,: hanc tu mihi vel vi, vel clam, vel precario Fac tradas (a jurid. formula),; cf. : qui propter avaritiam clam depositum non reddidit,: clam mussitantes,; : praemissis confestim clam cohortibus,; : ille Sychaeum Clam ferro incautum superat,stealthily,: nec dic quid doleas, clam tamen usque dole,: cui te commisit alendum Clam,; cf. al.—
Esp.
With advv.; with furtim, ; with furtive,; with occulte,; poet. with tacitus: tacito clam venit illa pede, and similar words,; ; cf.: strepito nullo clam reserare fores,; opp. palam, Enn. l. l.; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; and opp. propalam,.—
With gen.: res exulatum at illam clam abibat patris, Ritschl (cf. λάθρη Λαομέδοντος, Hom. Il. 5, 269).—
Clam est, with subj.-clause (cf. II. B. infra): meretricem commoneri Quam sane magni referat, nil clam'st,.—
Prep., without the knowledge of, unknown to, constr. with abl. or acc.

(in the class. per. very rare), of the quiet, placid, pleasant state of the air, wind, or weather, mild, calm, soft, gentle ( = the class. placidus, quietus): undae clementi flamine pulsae, * : clementior Auster vela vocat,: aura Favoni,; cf. ; : clementior dies,: clementior Arctos,: clementiores plagae (opp. Septentrio),.—Hence,

Trop.
Of a calm, unexcited, passionless state of mind, quiet, mild, gentle, tranquil, kind (syn.: placidus, lenis): clementem vocabo non in alieno dolore facilem, sed eum, qui cum suis stimulis exagitetur, non prosilit, etc.,: egit semper vitam... clemens, placidus,: vita urbana atque otium, (cf. with : vita quieta atque otiosa): ille suam semper egit vitam in otio, in conviviis: clemens, placidus,; (cf. the passages under clementia, cited from Flor.): cupio, patres conscripti, me esse clementem: cupio in tantis rei publicae periculis me non dissolutum videri,: etsi satis clemens sum in disputando, tamen interdum soleo subirasci,: (Arimphaeis) ritus clementes,.—
Transf. to animals. tame, domesticated: clementius genus columbarum

(opp. agrestes), .—

Specif.
Mild in respect to the faults and failures of others, i. e. forbearing, indulgent, compassionate, merciful (class.; syn.: mitis, benignus, humanus, lenis, facilis, indulgens; opp.: crudelis, inhumanus, asper al.): clementi (mi) animo ignoscet,; : judices et misericordes,; cf. * ; : vir et contra audaciam fortissimus et ab innocentiā clementissimus,; : legis interpres,: dominus facilis et clemens,: justa et clemens servitus,: castigatio,: clementior sententia,.—More unusual: rumor, i. e. non nimius, mild, mitigated, πρᾶος (acc. to P.), .—
Poet. of places: pars (insulae) ratibus clemens,accessible,.—Adv.: clē-menter.
(Acc. to I. A.) Gently, softly, mildly: non desiit adsidue tremere Campania, clementius quidem, sed ingenti damno,: agitant venti oleas,: spirant clementius Austri,.—So of moderate, slow action gen.: Eu. Sequere sis. Ch. Sequor. Eu. Clementer quaeso; calces deteris,; so ; . —
(Acc. to I. B. 2.) By degrees, gradually, gently: clementer et molliter assurgens collis,; cf. : editum jugum,; ; : accedere,; cf. in comp.: explorare, si quā Appennini juga clementius adirentur,.—
(Acc. to II. A.) Quietly, placidly, tranquilly, calmly: accipere aliquid clementius aequo, * : si quid est factum clementer, ut dissolute factum criminer,: leniter hominem clementerque accepit,, § 86: ferre aliquid,: consolationes clementer admotae,: quo id pacto fieri possit clementissime,: leo caudam clementer et blande movet,.—
(Acc. to II. B.) With forbearance, mildly, with indulgence: clementer et moderate jus dicere,: clementer a consule accepti,: clementer ductis militibus,i.e. peacefully, without plundering,.— Comp.: clementius tractare aliquem,.—Sup.: clementissime scribere de aliquo,: qui victoriā civili clementissime usus est,.
